newsitem.title: UK: Spectacular rally in coffee turns volatile.
newsitem.headline: Spectacular rally in coffee turns volatile.

text.p: World coffee prices turned volatile on Friday but traders were wary just yet of calling an end to the spectacular rally that has taken them up around 50 percent in value since early January.
New York Arabica coffee futures rode a rollercoaster when speculative profit-taking and options-related selling sent prices reeling from new contract highs hit earlier in the session.
March rose to 182.50 cents per pound then dropped almost to technical support at $176 before edging up again. Traders said the market is likely to stay volatile.
London Robusta coffee rose as high as $1,705 per tonne before easing to close up just $15 on the day at $1,675.
Origin countries sold in to the rally in London.
"It's churning close to the top but we're not predicting where the top is," said a London trader.

The rally on coffee which has led roasters to hike retail prices in Europe and the United States is based on a perception that stocks are low and that Brazil may have a smaller crop, as well as labour unrest in Colombia.
The market was likely to be supported by an ongoing strike there after 17 hours of heated bargaining between union leaders and government ministers ended in a deadlock on Thursday.
In other news, German coffee roaster Kraft Jacobs Suchard (KJS) said it could not rule out further retail price increases if the rally in futures prices was maintained.
Gold edged up on Friday but most other world commodity markets were little changed to easier as traders squared their books ahead of the US President's Day holiday on Monday.

Gold was indicated late in the London day above $346.50 per ounce or some $10 above the 3-3/4 year low to which it sank earlier in the week. Dealers say that the bullion market remains wary and may again be vulnerable speculative sales.

Confidence in gold ebbed on fears that other central banks might follow those of Belgium and the Netherlands in selling bulion from reserves. The Belgian central bank said on Thursday it would not sell any more gold.
Germany's BHF-Bank said on a report published on Friday that commodity prices should undergo consolidation at high levels in 1997 on the basis of global economic growth of around four percent.
But price rises would be limited because the supply of raw materials was likely to expand in a "textbook" response to the high prices.
Crude oil prices may average slightly below $20 per barrel after $20.5 in 1996 because of an easing of the recent tightness, the bank said.
In food commodities, the bank predicted 1997 price rises in tight coffee markets and in grains, where stocks were still low.
Grain prices last year rose by 21 percent, oilseeds and oils by 13 percent while combined cocoa, coffee and sugar prices were off 19 percent.
The bank based the figures on a 28-product commodities index developed by the HWWA Institute for Economic Research, Hamburg, which measures dollar prices against 1975.
